props.title: Boiling Point
props.initialSlug: Cop goes undercover to bust deadly drug ring

sections.content: **Boiling Point** (1990) represents a fascinating entry in Wesley Snipes' early career, blending noir elements with gritty street crime. Director James B. Harris, who previously produced Kubrick classics like **The Killing** (1956), crafts a slow-burn thriller about Treasury agent Jimmy Mercer (Snipes) hunting the killers of his partner. The film shares DNA with other undercover cop dramas of the era like Deep Cover (1992) and New Jack City (1991), but takes a more methodical approach focused on mounting tension rather than action spectacle.

sections.content: Harris adapts the Japanese novel "Money Men" with a distinctly American noir sensibility, letting Dennis Hopper steal scenes as Red Diamond, a manipulative ex-con running small-time scams. The film's methodical pacing and focus on character psychology recalls **The Friends of Eddie Coyle** (1973) and **To Live and Die in L.A.** (1985), examining the blurred lines between cop and criminal through extended dialogue scenes and brewing tension rather than gunfights.

The early 90s marked a crucial period for crime films examining police corruption and moral ambiguity. While Bad Lieutenant (1992) took an extreme approach and **Internal Affairs** (1990) went for glossy thriller territory, **Boiling Point** sits somewhere in between - a character study masquerading as a revenge film that's more interested in the psychological toll of undercover work than traditional action beats. sections.content: **Boiling Point** bridges the gap between 70s character-driven crime films and the more kinetic 90s police thrillers. Its DNA can be traced through later works like **One False Move** (1992) and **Fresh** (1994), which similarly prioritize atmosphere and character over action. The film's influence on the genre helped pave the way for morally complex police dramas like **Training Day** (2001) and **Narc** (2002).
